meta.author: Dolman
meta.purpose: Essential oils used in cleaning. Cleaning efficacy and population safety are recorded as SEPARATE, independently levelled claims, because 'cleans well' and 'safe around a cat' are different questions and merging them into one score is the most common way a transparency tool misleads.
meta.disclaimer: Not veterinary or medical advice. Population flags describe documented hazard in the cited literature at the concentrations and routes those sources studied. Dose, formulation strength, ventilation, and route of exposure all change the risk. Absence of a flag is not proof of safety.
meta.note_2023_1545: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1545 expanded the EU labelled fragrance-allergen list from 24 to over 80 entries and is in force for new products from 31 July 2026. Geranium oil and pinene are both newly labelled allergens, which affects the Geranium and Pine entries. Per Linnea, CCI-009 rev1.

children.basis: Pediatric deaths are documented, not inferred. Two infants poisoned from pennyroyal-containing mint tea: an 8-week-old died of fulminant hepatic failure with cerebral edema and hepatocellular necrosis, with serum-confirmed pulegone and menthofuran. A separate 16-month-old died with central zonal necrosis. Route caveat: the documented route is ingestion, not household-cleaning exposure.

pregnancy.basis: Pennyroyal oil was used historically as an abortifacient and contains around 85% pulegone, which the liver converts to hepatotoxic metabolites. Documented cases include ingestion specifically to induce abortion, with massive hepatic necrosis and death.

sensitive.basis: Described as a direct cytotoxin. Acute hepatic necrosis and multiorgan failure are documented; around 10 mL of pennyroyal oil is associated with moderate to severe toxicity.

Pennyroyal.note: The most serious pregnancy flag in this catalog. Historically used to induce abortion, with documented harm. Not a household cleaning oil, included so nobody assumes it is one.

Thieves.owner: Young Living Essential Oils (private, MLM) — verify before publishing

degreasing.basis: Contains lemon, a verified degreaser. The blend as a whole has not been measured for degreasing in any source located.

antimicrobial.basis: Contains clove, cinnamon and eucalyptus, all of which show documented antimicrobial activity individually. An oil blend showed stronger biocidal action than single oils in an in-situ comparison, so a synergistic effect is plausible. Not measured for this blend.

cats.basis: Four of the five components (clove, lemon, cinnamon, eucalyptus) are individually named in the published list of oils known to poison cats. Cats are described as more sensitive than dogs because they lack glucuronyl transferase and are especially sensitive to phenolic compounds, which clove and cinnamon contain.

dogs.basis: Cinnamon and eucalyptus are named among oils known to poison dogs; clove oil is described as toxic to dogs and capable of causing vomiting, diarrhoea and liver damage.

birds.basis: Cats and birds are described as at particular risk from essential oil toxicosis.

sensitive.basis: Contains declared fragrance allergens eugenol (clove), cinnamaldehyde (cinnamon) and limonene (lemon), and dermal application guidance is to dilute 1 drop in 4 drops of carrier oil. Declared allergen status confirmed against Regulation (EC) 1223/2009 Annex III.

claim_conflict.manufacturer_claim: The Thieves Household Cleaner product sheet states it is 'great to use around the whole family, including pets and children'.
claim_conflict.toxicology_finding: Four of the five oils in the blend are individually named in published veterinary lists of essential oils that cause poisoning in cats, and two are named for dogs. The veterinary literature states that risk increases with concentration and that cats and birds are at particular risk.
claim_conflict.note: Recorded as a tension, not as a verdict. Dose matters: a diluted household cleaner is a lower exposure than neat oil, and a capful-per-bucket dilution is not the same as applying the oil. The manufacturer's claim is asserted without a cited basis; the veterinary finding is cited. Both are shown.

naming_legend.claim: Named for 15th-century French thieves who robbed plague victims, said to have protected themselves with an aromatic blend of clove, rosemary and other botanicals.
naming_legend.basis: The manufacturer's own material introduces it as 'Legend says'. Three differing versions appear across their own product pages: four 15th-century French thieves; 14th-century perfumers and spice traders who traded the formula for leniency; and a version naming a different century. This is folklore, not documented history.
naming_legend.note: The folk recipe was vinegar-based. The modern blend contains no vinegar and is a proprietary oil blend inspired by the story.

Thieves.note: The single best demonstration piece in this database. It shows the certainty system working across four layers at once: a legend presented as a name, a composition that differs from the legend, a safety claim asserted without a source, and a toxicology record that says otherwise.
